claims.text: High configurational entropy promotes formation of a single, homogeneous alloy phase in noble metal–based HEA nanomaterials.
A homogeneous alloy phase creates synergistic electronic interactions among constituent metal sites.
Uniform alloy structures provide improved and more reliable catalytic performance than reduced-entropy compositions.
Compositions with reduced configurational entropy tend to phase-segregate.
An equiatomic formulation has higher configurational entropy than a deliberately non-equiatomic formulation of the same alloy system.
Rapid thermal annealing in an inert atmosphere can provide a processing window favorable to HEA formation.
High configurational entropy during synthesis suppresses phase separation.
Suppression of phase separation produces a uniformly mixed alloy.
Uniform mixing promotes synergistic electronic interactions among noble metals.
Synergistic electronic interactions optimize electron-density redistribution at catalytic active sites.
Optimized electron-density redistribution enhances catalytic activity.
The equiatomic sample will have a more homogeneous, single-phase structure than the non-equiatomic sample under identical synthesis conditions.
The equiatomic sample will exhibit higher catalytic activity, such as higher turnover frequency or lower activation energy, than the non-equiatomic sample.
The non-equiatomic sample will show phase segregation and reduced catalytic performance.
The proposed relationship is limited to synthesis conditions that preserve nanostructured HEA formation and remain below thermal-stability limits associated with bulk phase separation.
The proposed relationship is limited to noble-metal catalysts synthesized by rapid thermal processing.
The magnitude of structural and catalytic differences may depend on the specific combination of metals.
